p.seg: The reason why the former kings taught
is why it is connected to Shào Gōng.
"Zhōu Nán"
and "Shào Nán"
are the way of the correct beginning,
the foundation of the kingly transformation.
Therefore, in "Guān Jū," happiness is derived from obtaining a virtuous woman to be a consort to a gentleman,
with concern focused on advancing the worthy and not being indulgent in her beauty;
lamenting the refined and graceful,
thinking of talented individuals,
and without a heart that injures goodness.
This is the meaning of "Guān Jū."
"Guānguān" cry the ospreys,
on the islet in the river.
The graceful and virtuous maiden
is a good match for the gentleman!
The uneven water-mallows,
are gathered to the left and right.
The graceful and virtuous maiden
is sought after waking and sleeping.
Not obtaining her after seeking,
waking and sleeping, he longs for her.
Oh, so long, so long!
He tosses and turns.
The uneven water-mallows,
are gathered to the left and right.
Yǎotiǎo shúnǚ,
qín sè yǒu zhī.
Cēncī xìngcài,
zuǒyòu mào zhī.
Yǎotiǎo shúnǚ,
zhōnggǔ yuè zhī.
"Guān Jū" has five stanzas, each with four lines.
Therefore, three stanzas are spoken of;
one stanza has four lines,
two stanzas have eight lines.
2 "Gé Tán"
"Gé Tán"
is about the foundation of the queen and concubines.
When the queen and concubines are in their parents' home,
their ambition is focused on the work of women;
practicing frugality and economy,
wearing washed and cleaned clothes;
respecting teachers and mentors;
then they can return to bring peace to their parents,
and transform the world with the way of women.
The kudzu spreads,
extending into the middle of the valley,
its leaves luxuriant.
The yellow bird flies,
Gathered on the shrubs,
their calls are jiē jiē.
The gé vine spreads,
extending into the central valley,
its leaves are lush and abundant.
We cut and boil it,
to make fine and coarse cloth,
wearing it without weariness.
I will tell the teacher,
I will tell them I am returning home.
Lightly wash my private clothes,
lightly wash my garments.
Should I wash or not?
I am returning to visit my parents!
"Gé Tán" (The Gé Vine), three stanzas,
each stanza of six lines.
3 "Juǎn Ěr" (Cocklebur)
"Juǎn Ěr" (Cocklebur) is the expression of the queen and consort's aspirations.
后妃之志也。
Moreover, she should assist the ruler,
seeking out the worthy and scrutinizing officials.
Understanding the hard work of her subordinates,
inwardly possessing the aspiration to promote the capable,
and without treacherous, biased, or private requests in her heart,
thinking about it morning and night,
to the point of worry and diligence.
Picking and picking cocklebur,
not filling a small basket.
Alas, I long for someone,
placed there on the Zhōu road!
Climbing that steep and rocky height,
my horse is weary and worn.
Let me pour from that golden *léi*,
so that I may not cherish these thoughts forever!
Climbing that high ridge,
my horse is black and yellow, exhausted.
Let me pour from that rhinoceros horn cup *sìgōng*,
so that I may not grieve forever!
Climbing that rocky hill,
my horse is ill,
my servant is sick.
What can I do but sigh!
"Juǎn'ěr" has four stanzas, each stanza with four lines.
4. "Jiū Mù"
"Jiū Mù" is about
the queen reaching out to those below her.
It speaks of her ability to reach out to those below,
and without a jealous heart.
In the south are bent trees,
with gé-lěi vines entwining them.
Happy is this jūn-zǐ!
May good fortune and blessings bring him peace.
In the south are bent trees,
with gé-lěi vines covering them.
Happy is this jūn-zǐ!
May good fortune and blessings attend him.
In the south are bent trees,
with gé-lěi vines winding around them.
Happy is this jūn-zǐ!
May good fortune and blessings complete him.
"Jiū Mù" has three stanzas, each with four lines.
5 "Zhōng Sī"
"Zhōng Sī" describes
the numerous descendants of the queen and concubines.
It says that if one is like the zhōng-sī grasshopper,
and is not jealous,
then one's descendants will be numerous.
The grasshopper's wings,
rustle and rustle.
May your children and grandchildren be abundant and flourishing!
The grasshopper's wings,
Buzzing they go.
May they bring forth descendants, continuously and abundantly!
The locusts fly,
in swarms they gather.
May they bring forth descendants, densely and numerously!
"Zhōng Sī," three stanzas,
four lines per stanza.
6 "Táo Yāo"
"Táo Yāo,"
(is a poem) inspired by the queens and consorts.
If there is no jealousy,
then men and women are proper,
marriage is timely, and the country has no widowers.
The peach tree is young and elegant,
Bright are its flowers.
This girl is going to her new home,
May she harmonize her household.
The peach tree is young and elegant,
Abundant is its fruit.
This girl is going to her new home,
May she harmonize her family.
The peach tree is young and elegant,
Its leaves are luxuriant.
This girl is going to her new home,
she will bring harmony to her family.
"Táo Yāo" has three stanzas, each stanza has four lines.
7 "Tù Jū" (Rabbit Net)
"Tù Jū,"
is about the transforming influence of the queen.
When the transforming influence of "Guān Jū" is practiced,
then no one will fail to love virtue,
and worthy people will be numerous.
Tightly woven is the rabbit net,
pegged into the ground with resounding blows.
Brave and strong are the warriors,
they are the shield and walls of the dukes and lords.
Tightly woven is the rabbit net,
set in the middle of the open road.
Brave and strong are the warriors,
they are the good companions of the dukes and lords.
Tightly woven is the rabbit net,
set in the middle of the forest.
Brave and strong are the warriors,
they are the heart and soul of the dukes and lords.
"Tù Jū" (Rabbit Trap) has three stanzas, each with four lines.
8 "Fú Yǐ" (Plantain)
"Fú Yǐ" (Plantain)
is about the beauty of the queen and consorts.
In times of peace
women are happy to have children.
Gathering, gathering plantain,
we are just beginning to gather it.
Gathering, gathering plantain,
we are just beginning to have it.
Gathering, gathering plantain,
we are just beginning to pick it up.
Gathering, gathering plantain,
we are just beginning to strip it.
Gathering, gathering plantain,
we are just beginning to hold it in our lap.
Gathering, gathering plantain,
we are just beginning to tuck it into our belt.
"Fú Yǐ" (Plantain) has three stanzas,
each with four lines.
9 "Hàn Guǎng" (The Hàn River is Wide)
《Hàn Guǎng》,
the reach of virtue's influence.
The Way of King Wénwáng was extended to the Southern states,
and the beauty of transformation practiced in the regions of the Jiāng and Hàn rivers,
without thoughts of transgressing ritual propriety,
sought for but unobtainable.
There are tall trees in the South,
under which one cannot rest.
There are roaming maidens on the Hàn River,
whom one cannot pursue with longing.
The Hàn River is so wide,
one cannot swim across it thinking.
The Jiāng River is so long,
one cannot raft across it thinking.
Tall and tangled are the cut firewood!
Someone is saying he will cut the *chǔ* (vitex).
Is that girl going home (in marriage)?
Someone is saying he will feed his horses.
The Hàn River is so wide,
one cannot swim across it thinking.
The Jiāng River is so long,
one cannot raft across it thinking.
Tall and tangled are the cut firewood!
Someone is saying he will cut the *lóu* (artemisia).
Is that girl going home (in marriage)?
Spoken of is the feeding of his colt.
The Hàn is so vast,
it cannot be swum across.
The Jiāng is so long,
it cannot be crossed by raft.
"Hàn Guǎng", three stanzas,
eight lines per stanza.
10 "Rǔ Fén"
"Rǔ Fén" signifies
the practice of moral transformation.
The transforming influence of King Wén extended to the state of Rǔ Fén, where women were able to
be concerned about their husbands,
and still encouraged them to be upright.
Following that Rǔ Fén,
we cut down the branches and twigs.
Not having seen my husband,
I am as distressed as if enduring hunger!
Following that Rǔ Fén,
we cut down the branches and young shoots.
Now that I have seen my husband,
will he not cast me off?
The bream has a red tail,
the royal house is like a fire.
Although it is like a fire,
my parents are very near!
"Rǔ Fén" (汝墳) consists of three chapters,
with each chapter containing four lines.
11 "Lín Zhī Zhǐ" (麟之趾)
"Lín Zhī Zhǐ" (麟之趾) is
a response to "Guān Jū" (關雎).
When the transformative influence of "Guān Jū" (關雎) prevails,
then there will be no transgressions against propriety in the world.
Even the sons of noble families in a declining age will be as trustworthy and sincere as when the young of the lín (麟) are plentiful.
"Lín zhī zhǐ (麟之趾),
abundant are the young lords.
Alas, the lín (麟)!"
"Lín zhī dìng (麟之定),
abundant are the noble surnames.
Alas, the lín (麟)!"
"Lín zhī jiǎo (麟之角),
abundant are the noble clans.
Alas, the lín (麟)!"
"Lín Zhī Zhǐ" (麟之趾) consists of three chapters,
with each chapter containing three lines.
The "Zhōu Nán" (周南) section of the Guó Fēng (國風) contains eleven poems,
comprising thirty-six chapters,
and one hundred and fifty-nine lines.
Guó Fēng (國風), Shào Nán (召南), second.
12. "Què Cháo" (Magpie's Nest)
"Què Cháo"
praises the virtue of the First Lady.
The ruler of the state accumulates virtuous deeds and merits to attain his noble position.
The First Lady rises from her family to share this position.
Only one whose virtue is like that of the shījiū (cuckoo or dove) is worthy to be his mate.
The magpie has built its nest,
But the cuckoo dwells in it.
This girl is going to her husband's home,
A hundred carriages meet her.
The magpie has built its nest,
But the cuckoo occupies it.
This girl is going to her husband's home,
A hundred carriages escort her.
The magpie has built its nest,
But the cuckoo fills it.
This girl is going to her husband's home,
A hundred carriages complete the procession.
"Què Cháo" has three stanzas,
each with four lines.
13. "Cǎi Fán" (Gathering White Artemisia)
"Cǎi Fán" (Gathering White Artemisia),
The wives and consorts do not neglect their duties.
If the wives and consorts can offer sacrifices,
then they do not neglect their duties.
Where do they gather the white artemisia?
In the pools and on the islets.
Where is it used?
In the affairs of dukes and lords.
Where do they gather the white artemisia?
In the midst of the streams.
Where is it used?
In the palaces of dukes and lords.
They are adorned in splendor,
Serving the public day and night.
They are adorned in abundance,
Soon they speak of returning home.
"Cǎi Fán" has three stanzas,
each stanza has four lines.
14. "Cǎo Chóng" (Grass Insects)
"Cǎo Chóng,"
The wives of high officials are able to use propriety to guard themselves.
The insects chirp softly,
The grasshoppers leap and jump.
Not yet seeing my lord (Jūnzǐ),
My heart is full of worry.
Now that I have seen him,
Now that I have met him,
My heart then calms down!
Ascending that southern mountain,
I say I will gather its ferns.
Not yet seeing my lord (Jūnzǐ),
My heart is deeply troubled.
Now that I have seen him,
Now that I have met him,
My heart then rejoices!
Ascending that southern mountain,
I say I will gather its vetch.
Not yet seeing my lord (Jūnzǐ),
My heart is sad and grieved.
Now that I have seen him,
Now that I have met him,
My heart then is at peace!
"Cǎo Chóng" (Grass Insects), three stanzas,
Each stanza has seven lines.
15 "Cǎi Pín" (Gathering Water-lily)
"Cǎi Pín" (Gathering Water-lily),
[Is about] the wife of a high official being able to follow the rules and regulations.
If one can follow the laws and standards,
then one can carry on the work of the ancestors
and participate in the ancestral sacrifices.
Where do we gather the water-lilies?
By the bank of the southern stream.
Where do we gather the pondweed?
In those transient pools.
Where do we put them?
In baskets and hampers.
Where do we cook them?
In tripods and pots.
Where do we set them out?
Under the window in the ancestral temple.
Who will personate the ancestor?
A reverent young woman.
"Cǎi Pín" (Gathering Water-lilies) has three stanzas,
each with four lines.
16 "Gān Táng" (The Sweet Pear Tree)
"Gān Táng,"
praises Zhào Bó.
Zhào Bó's teachings
were clear in the southern states.
Luxuriant is the sweet pear tree,
Do not cut it, do not fell it.
Shào Bó camped beneath it!
Luxuriant is the sweet pear tree,
Do not cut it, do not spoil it.
Shào Bó rested beneath it!
Luxuriant is the sweet pear tree,
Do not cut it, do not break it.
Shào Bó enjoyed it!
"Gāntáng" has three stanzas,
Each stanza has three lines.
17 "Xínglù"
"Xínglù" is about Shào Bó
hearing lawsuits.
The customs of decline and disorder were subtle,
and the teachings of integrity and trustworthiness flourished,
so that strong and violent men could not violate virtuous women.
Damp and heavy is the dew on the road.
Do I not rise early and late?
(Yet) I am told that traveling makes much dew!
Who says the sparrow has no horns?
How else could it pierce my roof?
Who says the woman has no home?
How else could she hasten my imprisonment?
Though you hasten my trial,
My family lacks enough!
Who says the rat has no teeth?
How could it pierce my wall?
Who says you, woman, have no home?
How could you hasten my lawsuit?
Though you hasten my lawsuit,
I will not follow you!
The *Xíng Lù* contains three stanzas,
One stanza has three lines,
Two stanzas each have six lines.
18 *Gāo Yáng*
*Gāo Yáng* represents the accomplishment of *Què Cháo*.
The country of Zhào Nán,
transformed by the policies of King Wén,
those in positions were all frugal and upright,
their virtue was like that of a lamb.
Lamb's skin,
White silk forms five strands?
Returning from public affairs for a meal,
So leisurely, so leisurely!
Lamb's leather,
White silk forms five selvages?
So leisurely, so leisurely,
Returning from public affairs for a meal.
When the lord retires from his meal.
The sewing of the lambskin robes,
With white silk in five strands?
How leisurely, how leisurely,
Retiring from his meal, from public affairs.
--"Gāo Yáng," three stanzas,
Each stanza of four lines.
19 "Yīn Qí Léi"
"Yīn Qí Léi" is a song to encourage righteousness.
The grand master of Zhào Nán,
travels far to engage in politics,
without leisure to settle down.
His family is able to sympathize with his hard work
and encourage him with righteousness.
Loud is the thunder,
On the south side of the Southern Mountain.
Why are you so distant, so estranged?
That no one dares to be idle?
O, you honorable gentleman,
Return! Return!
Loud is the thunder,
On the south side of the Southern Mountain.
Why are you so distant, so estranged?
No one dares to take a moment to rest!
Dignified gentlemen,
Return, oh, return!
The thunder rumbles loudly,
On the side of the Southern Mountain.
Why do you leave and separate from us,
With no one daring to take a moment to rest?
Dignified gentlemen,
Return, oh, return!
The thunder rumbles loudly,
At the foot of the Southern Mountain.
Why do you leave and separate from us,
With no one daring to take a moment to settle?
Dignified gentlemen,
Return, oh, return!
"Yīn Qí Léi" has three stanzas,
each with six lines.
20 "Biāo Yǒu Méi"
"Biāo Yǒu Méi" concerns
men and women acting at the proper time.
The state of Shào Nán was influenced by King Wén's civilization,
and men and women were able to act at the proper time.
The plums are falling,
Only seven are left.
Seek me, you many gentlemen,
Dài qí jí xī! When the auspicious time arrives!
Biāo yǒu méi, The plums are falling,
Qí shí sān xī. Only three are left on the branch.
Qiú wǒ shù shì, Let those gentlemen who seek me,
Dài qí jīn xī! Do so now!
Biāo yǒu méi, The plums are falling,
Qǐng kuāng jì zhī. Let them fill their shallow baskets.
Qiú wǒ shù shì, Let those gentlemen who seek me,
Dài qí wèi zhī! Do so while there is still time!
"Biāo Yǒu Méi" three stanzas,
four lines per stanza.
21 "Xiǎo Xīng"
"Xiǎo Xīng" means
kindness extending to inferiors.
The First Lady has no jealous or envious conduct,
and is kind to her humble concubines,
allowing them to approach the ruler.
She knows that their fates have high and low distinctions,
and is able to be completely sincere.
Huì bǐ xiǎo xīng, Those twinkling little stars,
sān wǔ zài dōng. Are scattered in the east.
Sù sù xiāo zhēng, We solemnly set out at night,
sù yè zài gōng. From dawn till dusk, we are on public duty.
Shí mìng bù tóng! Truly, our fates are different!
Huì bǐ xiǎo xīng, Those twinkling little stars,
It is like being involved with Mǎo (the Pleiades).
Hastily traveling at night,
embracing quilts and coverlets.
This is truly an unavoidable fate!
"Xiǎo Xīng" (Little Stars), two stanzas,
each stanza five lines.
22 "Jiāng Yǒu Sì" (The River Has Side-Streams)
"Jiāng Yǒu Sì" (The River Has Side-Streams),
praising the concubine.
Diligent and without complaint,
the principal wife is able to regret her errors.
In the time of King Wén,
between the Jiāng and Tuó rivers,
there was a principal wife who did not treat her concubine as fulfilling the required number;
the concubine encountered hardship and had no complaint,
and the principal wife also regretted it herself.
The river has side-streams,
that person is going home,
but does not include me.
Does not include me?
Afterwards, she will regret it!
The river has sandbanks,
that person is going home,
but does not involve me.
Does not involve me?
其後也處！ Afterwards, he settles down!
Jiāng yǒu Tuó, The Jiāng River has the Tuó.
zhī zǐ guī, That man is going home,
bù wǒ guò. He doesn't come to see me.
bù wǒ guò? He doesn't come to see me?
qí xiào yě gē! His whistling is like singing!
"Jiāng Yǒu Sì" sān zhāng, "Jiāng Yǒu Sì" has three stanzas,
zhāng wǔ jù. Each stanza has five lines.
23 "Yě Yǒu Sǐ Jūn" 23 "Yě Yǒu Sǐ Jūn" (There is a Dead Deer in the Wilds)
"Yě Yǒu Sǐ Jūn", "Yě Yǒu Sǐ Jūn" (There is a Dead Deer in the Wilds),
wù wú lǐ yě. detests the absence of propriety.
Tiānxià dà luàn, The world is in great disorder,
qiáng bào xiāng líng, the strong and violent bully each other,
suì chéng yín fēng. and consequently, licentious customs arise.
Bèi Wén Wáng zhī huà, Influenced by the teachings of King Wén,
suī dāng luàn shì, even in times of chaos,
yóu wù wú lǐ yě. they still detest the absence of propriety.
Yě yǒu sǐ jūn, There is a dead deer in the wilds,
bái máo bāo zhī. Wrapped with white rushes.
Yǒu nǚ huái chūn, There is a girl full of springtime desire,
jí shì yòu zhī. A good man is enticing her.
Lín yǒu pú sù, There are small trees in the forest,
yě yǒu sǐ lù, There is a dead deer in the wilds,
bái máo chún shù. Bound purely with white rushes.
A girl like jade!
Leisurely and graceful!
Do not touch my handkerchief!
Do not let the shaggy dog bark!
"Yě Yǒu Sǐ Jūn" (There is a Dead Roe in the Wild) has three stanzas,
two stanzas of four lines,
one stanza of three lines.
24 "Hé Bǐ Nóng Yǐ" (How Luxuriant)
"Hé Bǐ Nóng Yǐ",
praises the beautiful royal daughter.
Although she is a royal daughter,
she is still married down to a feudal lord;
her carriages and robes are not those of her husband,
but one rank below the queen,
yet she still upholds the way of a wife to achieve solemn and harmonious virtue.
How luxuriant!
The flowers of the Chinese flowering crabapple.
Why are they not solemn and harmonious?
The carriages of the royal daughter!
How luxuriant!
The blossoms are like peaches and plums.
The grandson of King Píng,
the son of the Marquis of Qí!
What does he fish with?
With silk line.
Qí hóu zhī zǐ,
Píng wáng zhī sūn!
"Hé Bǐ Nóng Yǐ" three chapters, four lines per chapter.
25 "Zōu Yú"
"Zōu Yú,"
the response to "Què Cháo."
When the transformation of "Què Cháo" is implemented,
and human relationships are rectified,
and the court is well-governed,
the world is purely imbued with the transformation of Wén Wáng.
Then all kinds of creatures flourish and multiply,
and hunting is conducted in due season.
If benevolence is like the Zōu Yú,
then the kingly way is accomplished.
That sprouting reed,
one shot, five sows.
Alas, the Zōu Yú!
That sprouting artemisia,
one shot, five young boars.
Alas, the Zōu Yú!
"Zōu Yú" two chapters,
three lines per chapter.
The state of Shào Nán: fourteen sections,
forty chapters,
one hundred and seventy-seven lines.
One hundred and seventy-seven sentences.
*Guófēng Běifēng* Third
26. "Bó Zhōu" (The Cypress Boat)
"Bó Zhōu" speaks of one who is benevolent but does not meet with good fortune.
During the time of Wèi Qǐnggōng,
benevolent people did not meet with good fortune,
and petty people were at their side.
Drifting is that cypress boat,
Also drifting in the current.
Shining bright and unable to sleep,
As if there were a hidden worry.
It's not that I don't have wine,
To frolic and to wander!
My heart is not a mirror,
It cannot contain everything.
I also have brothers,
But I cannot rely on them.
When I thinly go to complain,
I meet with their anger.
My heart is not a stone,
It cannot be turned!
My heart is not a mat,
It cannot be rolled up!
Dignified and composed,
beyond reproach!
My heart is deeply troubled,
resentment towards the petty people.
Encountering misfortune so often,
enduring no small amount of insult.
Quietly pondering it,
my dreams are filled with despair!
The sun and the moon pass by!
Why do they alternate and fade?
My heart is full of sorrow,
like unwashed clothes!
Quietly pondering it,
I cannot take flight!
"Cypress Boat" has five stanzas,
each stanza six lines.
27 "Green Robe"
"Green Robe,"
(is about) Zhuāng Jiāng of Wèi grieving for herself.
Concubines presumptuously rise,
the wife loses her position,
and thus this poem was made.
Green is the robe,
a green robe with a yellow lining.
My heart is full of sorrow,
when will it ever cease?
Green is the robe,
a green robe with a yellow skirt.
My heart is full of sorrow,
when will it ever end?
Green is the silk,
Which you are mending.
I think of the ancients,
May they be without fault!
Fine linen and coarse linen,
Cold and windy.
I think of the ancients,
They truly capture my heart!
"Lǜ Yī" has four stanzas,
Each stanza has four lines.
28 "Yàn Yàn"
"Yàn Yàn" is about Wèi Zhuāng Jiāng seeing off a concubine being sent home.
Wèi Zhuāng Jiāng (衛莊姜) sent back a concubine.
Swallows fly swiftly,
Their feathers are uneven.
This lady is going to her home,
Sent far away into the fields.
Gazing, I cannot reach her,
Tears fall like rain!
Swallows fly swiftly,
They flutter and soar.
This girl is going to her new home,
far away she is to be sent.
I strain to see her, but cannot reach her,
I stand and weep!
Swallows fly about,
uttering their calls above and below.
This girl is going to her new home,
I escort her far to the south.
I strain to see her, but cannot reach her,
truly it troubles my heart!
Daughter of the Zhòng family, Rèn!
Her heart is deep and still.
Always gentle and kind,
virtuous and careful in her conduct.
The late ruler's thoughts,
are what encourage me, the lonely one!
"Yàn Yàn," four stanzas,
each stanza six lines.
29 "Rì Yuè" (Sun and Moon)
"Rì Yuè," [is about] Zhuāng Jiāng of Wèi
grieving for herself.
Encountering the troubles of Zhōu Xū,
grieving that she did not receive a response from the late ruler,

The feasting of youth,

Not thinking of turning back,

80 "The Lambskin Coat"
"Gāo Qiú"
is a satire on the court. It speaks of the ancient gentlemen who influenced their court through their demeanor.
The lambskin robe is as if soaked,
truly upright and dignified.
That man,
he would sacrifice his life without changing!
The lambskin robe is adorned with leopard,
exceedingly martial and strong.
That man,
he is the Director of Uprightness of the state!
The lambskin robe is elegant,
the three tassels are bright,
that man,
he is the paragon of the state!
"Gāo Qiú" has three stanzas,
each stanza has four lines.
81 "Zūn Dà Lù"
"Zūn Dà Lù"
is about longing for the virtuous gentleman.
When Zhuāng Gōng lost his way,
the virtuous gentleman left him,
and the people of the state longed for him.
Walking along the great road,
I take hold of your sleeve.
Do you dislike me?
Is it because I am not diligent in the past?
Follow the great path, let us hold each other's hands.
Do you hate me?
Is it because I am not diligent in loving you?
“Following the Great Road,” two stanzas,
each stanza four lines.
82 “The Wife Says, The Rooster Crows”
"The Wife Says, The Rooster Crows,"
is a satire against one who does not delight in virtue. It uses the ancient meaning to satirize the present where one does not delight in virtue but loves sensuality.
The wife says, "The rooster crows,"
the husband says, "It is still dark."
"Get up and look at the night,
the bright stars are shining.
"We shall soar and fly about,
shoot ducks and geese."
"When you shoot and hit them,
I will cook them for you.
When they are prepared, let us drink wine,
and grow old together.
With zithers and lutes at hand,
may all be quiet and good.”
"Knowing that you are coming,
I give you mixed pendants as a gift.
Knowing that you are compliant,
I give you mixed pendants to inquire.
Knowing that you love me,
I give you mixed pendants in return."
*Nǚ Yuē Jī Míng* (The Wife Says, "The Rooster Crows") has three stanzas,
each stanza with six lines.
83 *Yǒu Nǚ Tóng Chē* (There is a Woman in the Carriage)
*Yǒu Nǚ Tóng Chē* (There is a Woman in the Carriage)
is to satirize Hū.
The people of Zhèng satirize Hū for not marrying a woman from Qí.
Crown Prince Hū once rendered service to Qí,
and the Marquis of Qí requested to give him his daughter in marriage.
The woman of Qí was virtuous, but he did not take her,
and ultimately, without the aid of a great state,
he was even driven out.
Therefore, the people of the state satirized him.
There is a woman in the carriage,
her face like the hibiscus flower.
She is about to soar and hover,
wearing jade pendants and jade ornaments.
That beautiful Mèng Jiāng,
is truly beautiful and elegant!
With a maiden traveling with me,
Her face is like the Shùn Yīng flower.
She is about to soar, about to fly,
The sound of her jade pendants is jiāng jiāng.
That beauty is Mèng Jiāng,
Her virtuous voice is not forgotten!
"Yǒu Nǚ Tóng Chē" (With a Maiden in My Carriage) has two stanzas,
Each stanza has six lines.
84 《Shān Yǒu Fú Sū》 (There is a Fú Sū on the Mountain)
"Shān Yǒu Fú Sū,"
Is satire on "hū."
Praising what is not praiseworthy.
There is a Fú Sū tree on the mountain,
There are lotus flowers in the marsh.
I do not see Zǐ Dū,
But instead, I see a mad rustic!
There are tall pines on the mountain,
There are roaming dragons in the marsh.
I do not see Zǐ Chōng,
But instead, I see a cunning child!
"Shān Yǒu Fú Sū" has two stanzas,
Each stanza has four lines.
85 《Tuò Xī》 (Oh, the Fallen Leaves!)
"Tuò Xī"
, is satire against hū (忽).
The ruler is weak and the ministers are strong,
not leading but merely echoing.
Fallen leaves, fallen leaves,
will the wind blow you?
Uncles and elders,
lead and I will follow you!
Fallen leaves, fallen leaves,
will the wind carry you away?
Uncles and elders,
lead and I will meet you!
"Tuò Xī" has two stanzas,
each stanza has four lines.
86 "Jiǎo Tóng"
"Jiǎo Tóng",
is satire against hū (忽).
Unable to plan affairs with worthy people,
powerful ministers act on their own authority.
That cunning youth,
will not speak with me.
It is because of you,
that I cannot eat.
That cunning youth,
will not eat with me,
Wéi zǐ zhī gù,
shǐ wǒ bù néng xī xī.
"Jiǎo Tóng", two stanzas,
four lines per stanza.
87 "Qiān Cháng"
"Qiān Cháng":
longing to see correctness.
A mad youth acts willfully, and the people of the state long for the great state to correct them.
Zǐ huì sī wǒ,
qiān cháng shè Zhēn.
Zǐ bù wǒ sī,
qǐ wú tā rén?
Kuáng tóng zhī kuáng yě qiě!
Zǐ huì sī wǒ,
qiān cháng shè Wěi.
Zǐ bù wǒ sī,
qǐ wú tā shì?
Kuáng tóng zhī kuáng yě qiě!
"Qiān Cháng", two stanzas,
five lines per stanza.
88 "Fēng"
"Fēng":
This is a satire on disorder.
The proper way of marriage is lacking;
the *yáng* initiates but the *yīn* does not harmonize;
the man goes but the woman does not follow.
O my handsome man (*Zǐ zhī Fēng xī*),
you wait for me in the lane!
I regret that I did not see you off!
O my splendid man (*Zǐ zhī Chāng xī*),
you wait for me in the hall!
I regret that I did not accompany you!
Wearing cotton under a hemp garment,
a brocade skirt under a hemp skirt.
Uncle, elder brother,
harness the carriage, let me go with you!
A brocade skirt under a hemp skirt,
wearing brocade under a hemp garment.
Uncle, elder brother,
harness the carriage, let me return with you!
"Fēng" has four stanzas,
two stanzas with three lines each,
two stanzas with four lines each.
89 "Dōng Mén Zhī Shàn"
"Dōng Mén Zhī Shàn"
is a satire on disorder.
It describes men and women who run off together without observing the proper rites.
At the altar of the East Gate, madder grows on the slope.
His house is so near,
but the man is so far away!
The chestnuts of the East Gate
are trampled by those who have families.
How could I not think of you?
But you do not come to me!
"Dōng Mén zhī Shàn" (東門之墠) has two stanzas,
each stanza has four lines.
90 "Fēng Yǔ" (風雨)
"Fēng Yǔ" (風雨) is
about longing for the junzi (君子, gentleman).
In a chaotic world,
one thinks of the junzi who does not change his principles.
The wind and rain are chilling, the cocks crow harmoniously.
Now that I have seen the junzi,
how can I not be at peace!
The wind and rain are soughing,
the cocks crow clamorously.
Now that I have seen the junzi,
how can I not be healed!
The wind and rain are as dark as night,
the cocks crow ceaselessly.
Now that I have seen the junzi,
Yún hú bù xǐ! How could I not be happy!
《Fēng Yǔ》 Three stanzas,
Zhāng sì jù. four lines per stanza.
91. 《Zǐ Jīn》
《Zǐ Jīn》,
Cì xuéxiào fèi yě. is a satire on the abandonment of schools.
Luànshì, In chaotic times,
Zé xuéxiào bù xiū yān. schools are not maintained.
Qīng qīng zǐ jīn, Green is your collar,
Yōu yōu wǒ xīn. Long, long is my longing.
Zòng wǒ bù wǎng, Even if I don't go,
Zǐ níng bù sì yīn? Won't you send me a message?
Qīng qīng zǐ pèi, Green is your jade pendant,
Yōu yōu wǒ sī. Long, long are my thoughts.
Zòng wǒ bù wǎng, Even if I don't go,
Zǐ níng bù lái? Won't you come?
Tiāo xī dá xī, Back and forth you go,
Zài chéngquè xī. At the city tower!
Yī rì bù jiàn, Not seeing you for a day,
Rú sān yuè xī! Is like three months!
《Zǐ Jīn》 Three stanzas,
Zhāng sì jù. four lines per stanza.
92. 《Yáng Zhī Shuǐ》
"Yáng zhī Shuǐ"
is a lament for the absence of loyal ministers.
The ruler laments that Hū, lacking loyal and good ministers,
ultimately met his death,
and therefore this poem was composed.
The water in the stream,
cannot carry a bundle of firewood?
In the end, there are few brothers,
only you and I remain.
Do not trust the words of others,
people will truly deceive you.
The water in the stream,
cannot carry a bundle of kindling?
In the end, there are few brothers,
only the two of us remain.
Do not trust the words of others,
people are truly untrustworthy!
"Yáng zhī Shuǐ" has two stanzas,
each stanza having six lines.
93 "Chū Qí Dōng Mén"
"Chū Qí Dōng Mén" is a lament for disorder.
The princes competed five times,
and warfare did not cease.
Men and women abandon each other,
and the people think of protecting their homes and families.
Going out from the east gate,
there are women like clouds.
Though they are like clouds,
they are not in my thoughts.
In white clothes and green kerchief,
let me be happy with you!
Going out from the outer gate,
there are women like rushes.
Though they are like rushes,
they are not in my thoughts.
In white clothes and madder-dyed kerchief,
let me find joy with you!
"Chū Qí Dōng Mén" (Going Out From the East Gate) has two stanzas,
each with six lines.
94 "Yě Yǒu Màn Cǎo" (Wilds Have Spreading Grass)
"Yě Yǒu Màn Cǎo"
is about longing to meet the right time.
The ruler's grace does not flow downwards,
and the people are impoverished by war.
Men and women miss their proper time,
and long for an unarranged meeting.
In the wilds there is spreading grass,
The dew is heavy.
There is a beautiful person,
With clear and bright eyes so gentle.
We met by chance,
Fulfilling my desire!
In the fields, there are spreading grasses,
The dew is abundant.
There is a beautiful person,
Gentle and bright-eyed.
We met by chance,
With you, all is good!
“Yě Yǒu Màn Cǎo” (Wild Grasses) has two stanzas,
Each stanza has six lines.
95 “Zhēn Wěi”
“Zhēn Wěi”
Is a satire on disorder.
War chariots do not rest,
Men and women abandon each other,
Lewd customs are widespread,
And no one can save them.
At the Zhēn (溱) and Wěi (洧) rivers,
The water flows vast and free.
Men and women,
Hold orchids in their hands.
The woman says, "Shall we watch?"
The man said he'd already been there.
"How about going to see?"
"Beyond the Wěi River,
truly it is spacious and joyful."
These men and women!
How they jest with each other,
presenting each other with peonies.
At the Zhēn and Wěi Rivers,
how clear and limpid the water is!
The men and women,
how numerous they are!
The woman said, "Shall we go see?"
The man said he'd already been there.
"How about going to see?"
"Beyond the Wěi River,
truly it is spacious and joyful."
These men and women!
How they will jest with each other,
presenting each other with peonies.
"Zhēn Wěi," two stanzas,
each stanza twelve lines.
In the state of Zhèng, there are twenty-one poems,
fifty-three stanzas,
two hundred and eighty-three lines.

96 "Jī Míng"
"Jī Míng"
is about thinking of a virtuous consort.
*Āi Gōng* was dissolute and negligent,
therefore it presents the way in which a virtuous consort and chaste women vigilantly assist each other day and night.
The rooster has already crowed,
is the court already full?
"It is not the rooster that crows,
it is the sound of flies."
The east is bright,
is the court already flourishing?
"It is not the east that is bright,
it is the light of the moon."
"Insects fly buzzing,
are you willing to dream with me?
You will soon be going home,
do not let me be hated by you!"
"Jī Míng" has three stanzas,
each stanza has four lines.
97 "Huán"
"Huán"
"Huán" is a satire on neglect.
Duke Āi was fond of hunting,
pursuing birds and beasts without satisfaction.
The people were influenced by this,
and it became a custom.
Being skilled in hunting was called being worthy,
and being skilled in chasing was called being good.
You, in your returning,
met me in the wilds of Náo.
Racing alongside, chasing two boars,
you greeted me, calling me quick.
You, in your flourishing,
met me on the road to Náo.
Racing alongside, chasing two stags,
you greeted me, calling me good.
You, in your prosperity,
met me on the sunny side of Náo.
Racing alongside, chasing two wolves,
you greeted me, calling me excellent.
"Huán" has three stanzas,
each stanza has four lines.
98 "Zhù"
"Zhuó" 《著》,
is a satire of the times.
The times are such that the groom does not personally fetch the bride.
Do you wait for me at the gate (zhù hū ér 著乎而)?
Do you fill your ears with plain silk (chōng ěr yǐ sù hū ér 充耳以素乎而),
and adorn them with jade flowers (shàng zhī yǐ qióng huá hū ér 尚之以瓊華乎而)?
Do you wait for me in the courtyard (tíng hū ér 庭乎而)?
Do you fill your ears with blue silk (chōng ěr yǐ qīng hū ér 充耳以青乎而),
and adorn them with gleaming jade (shàng zhī yǐ qióng yíng hū ér 尚之以瓊瑩乎而)?
Do you wait for me in the hall (táng hū ér 堂乎而)?
Do you fill your ears with yellow silk (chōng ěr yǐ huáng hū ér 充耳以黃乎而),
and adorn them with jade ornaments (shàng zhī yǐ qióng yīng hū ér 尚之以瓊英乎而)?
"Zhuó" 《著》 has three stanzas,
with three lines per stanza.
99 "Dōng Fāng Zhī Rì" 《東方之日》
"Dōng Fāng Zhī Rì" 《東方之日》,
is a satire of decline.
The ruler and ministers have lost the Way,
and men and women engage in licentious affairs,
unable to be transformed by ritual propriety.
O sun rising in the east (dōng fāng zhī rì xī 東方之日兮)!
That beautiful girl (bǐ shū zhě zǐ 彼姝者子),
is in my room (zài wǒ shì xī 在我室兮)!
Being in my room (zài wǒ shì xī 在我室兮)!
Lǚ wǒ jí xī.
The moon of the east!
That lovely girl,
is at my gate.
Is at my gate!
I tread, I hasten.
"Dōngfāng zhī Rì," two stanzas,
each stanza five lines.
100 "Before the East is Bright"
"Dōngfāng Wèi Míng,"
is an invective against those who are without measure.
The court's rising and resting have no measure,
orders and decrees are not timely,
the Pitcher Master cannot manage his office.
Before the east is bright,
putting on clothes upside down.
Upside down and reversed,
the duke himself summons them.
Before the east has dried,
putting on lower and upper garments upside down.
Reversed and upside down,
the duke himself commands them.
*zhé liǔ fán pǔ,*
*kuáng fū qú qú.*
*bù néng chén yè,*
*bù sù zé mò.*
"Dōng Fāng Wèi Míng" in three stanzas,
each stanza has four lines.
101. "Nán Shān"
"Nán Shān"
is a criticism of Duke Xiāng.
The behavior of birds and beasts,
engaging in incest with his younger sister.
A high official, encountering this wickedness,
composed a poem and left him.
The Southern Mountain is lofty,
the male fox walks leisurely.
The roads of Lǔ are broad,
the Qi maiden returns.
Since you said you would stay,
why do you still yearn to leave?
Sandals of hemp are in pairs,
cap strings hang doubly down.
The roads of Lǔ are broad,
the Qi maiden stays.
Since you said you would stay,
why then do you follow others?
How does one plant flax?
In rows and across the fields.
How does one take a wife?
One must certainly inform one's parents.
